topic: A tech explainer: what happens between typing a URL and seeing the page. Stacknotes is a made-up example brand.

slides.title: What happens when you open a website
slides.subtitle: From pressing Enter to the first pixels: every lookup, handshake and request, in order.

slides.title: First, find the address
slides.body: Networks route by IP address, *not by name*. Unless a cache already knows the answer, your device asks a DNS resolver which address belongs to the name you typed, for example 203.0.113.7.

slides.title: Root, then .com, then the domain
slides.caption: With nothing cached, the resolver asks a root server, then a .com server, then the domain’s name server.

slides.label: named root servers at the top of DNS
slides.note: Named a to m. Each runs as many anycast copies worldwide, so your query reaches a nearby one.

items.title: TCP handshake
items.text: Three packets: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. HTTP/3 uses QUIC instead.

items.title: TLS handshake
items.text: Keys agreed, certificate checked: one round trip in TLS 1.3.

items.title: HTTP request
items.text: The browser sends GET with headers like Host and cookies.

items.title: Server response
items.text: A status code such as 200, headers, then the HTML.

slides.title: Then the browser draws
slides.body: It parses the HTML into the DOM and the CSS into the CSSOM, works out the layout and paints the pixels. Every script, style sheet and image it finds can *start another request*.

slides.quote: Slow page? Don’t guess. Open your browser’s network panel: the waterfall shows how long each step took, from DNS lookup to the last byte.
slides.author: Stacknotes

slides.title: The classic interview question, answered
slides.text: Next time someone asks, walk them through it: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, then the render.

caption:
You press Enter, and a moment later the page is there. Here is everything that happens in between.

DNS lookup, TCP and TLS handshakes, the HTTP request and the render, one slide each.
